title: Enforcement fear can reduce victim reporting while reported crime stays flat
source_unit: Census CES Working Paper 26-23, using the Secure Communities policy and linked crime and victim-reporting evidence
geography: United States; immigrant communities, Hispanic victims, local law-enforcement jurisdictions, and policy rollout periods

observations.period: Secure Communities policy period; paper published April 2026

reporting.value: the policy reduced the likelihood that Hispanic victims reported crimes to police

reported_crime.value: the number of reported crimes was unchanged because opposing changes were masked

elasticity.value: a 10% decline in victim reporting increased offending by 7.9%

mechanism.value: deportation fear reduced reporting and the reporting decline drove the increase in offending

observations.method: The authors study the Secure Communities enforcement policy and combine policy variation with crime and victim-reporting evidence to estimate reporting and offending relationships.
observations.uncertainty: This is a Census CES working paper and not a Census Bureau endorsement. The abstract does not establish that every enforcement policy, jurisdiction, immigrant group, or crime category behaves the same way. Reported-crime stability cannot be read as stable victimization or stable public safety.
observations.subgroup: Hispanic victims and immigrant communities exposed to Secure Communities; subgroup differences by place, legal status, crime type, age, gender, and institutional contact require separate analysis.
observations.counterinterpretation: Changes in police practice, local crime conditions, migration, community organization, or enforcement intensity could affect reporting and offending together. A decline in reporting may reflect fear, distrust, cost, perceived futility, or alternative support routes; the public abstract does not separate all of these channels.

related_sources.claim: The official paper provides the policy design, reporting analysis, offending estimates, and caveats behind the abstract.

boundary: This record adds a policy-climate-to-reporting-to-public-safety pathway. It does not establish universal effects, identify every reason for nonreporting, measure all victimization, or prove later trust, civic action, or durable institutional legitimacy.
